introduction.text: Piazza del Campidoglio is a historic square on Rome's Capitoline Hill, redesigned by Michelangelo in the 16th century to serve as a civic center and showcase Rome's imperial heritage.

history.description: The Palazzo dei Conservatori was originally built in 1453 by Pope Nicholas V on the site of a 6th‑century temple.
The Capitoline Museums were founded in 1471 when Pope Sixtus IV donated key statues, including the Capitoline Wolf.
The square was redesigned by Michelangelo between 1534 and 1538 at the behest of Pope Paul III to impress Emperor Charles V.
The square’s oval pavement and star pattern were completed in 1546, reflecting Michelangelo’s geometric vision.
The Palazzo Nuovo was constructed in 1603 and finished in 1654, completing the symmetrical ensemble.
In 1940, Antonio Muñoz completed the paving of the square according to Michelangelo’s design.
The Cordonata ramp was built in the 16th century to allow horse riders to ascend the hill.

design.description: Michelangelo’s redesign turned the square’s orientation toward St. Peter’s Basilica, moving the civic focus from the Forum.
The double staircase (Cordonata) provides a dramatic ascent to the Palazzo Senatorio, a hallmark of Renaissance urban design.
The oval pavement features a twelve‑pointed star at its centre, a geometric motif that guides visitors to the equestrian statue.
The façades of the Palazzo dei Conservatori and Palazzo Nuovo were redesigned with giant order pilasters and balustraded cornices, creating visual harmony.
The Cordonata ramp is decorated with statues of the Tiber and Nile river gods, symbolising Rome’s dominion over the seas.

art.description: The equestrian statue of Marcus Aurelius, originally placed in the square, is a bronze copy of the original kept in the museum.
The Capitoline Wolf sculpture, donated by Pope Sixtus IV in 1471, is displayed in the Palazzo dei Conservatori.
The marble statues of the Tiber and Nile river gods flank the staircase, representing Rome’s maritime power.
